The Southern cotton rat Sigmodon hirsutus is a medium-sized cricetid rodent inhabiting grassy and shrubby habitats from southern Mexico to northwestern South America. Neonates of this species weigh approximately 6.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 6.2 grams], a value drawn from comparative data on the closely related Sigmodon hispidus. This initial mass is modest relative to the ultimate body size attained by adult females, which reaches an average of 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams], though field surveys have documented a range between 113 and 198 grams. Such variation in adult mass likely reflects differences in local habitat quality and seasonal food availability across the species' broad geographic range. The relatively low birth mass compared to the adult female mass suggests that prenatal investment per offspring is constrained, a pattern common among species that produce multiple litters per season. This reproductive strategy is consistent with that of other grassland rodents facing high predation pressure, where rapid population turnover is favored over extended maternal investment in individual young.

Reproduction in Sigmodon hirsutus is characterized by litter sizes ranging from five to twelve pups [N_R_i = litter sizes ranging from five to twelve pups] and a frequency of approximately one to two litters per year [F_R_i = approximately one to two litters per year]. Gestation lasts approximately 35 days [tg = approximately 35 days] under these thermal conditions, a duration that is typical for rodents of at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]this body size. The combination of a moderate gestation period, moderately large litter sizes, and a single or double annual reproductive event places this species at an intermediate position along the fast-slow continuum of mammalian life histories. Females invest considerable energy in each litter, with the total mass of a typical litter representing a substantial fraction of maternal body mass.

Postnatal development proceeds through a series of well-defined stages in the Southern cotton rat. The weaning period, defined as the time since birth at which offspring achieve nutritional independence from maternal milk, occurs at 15 days after birth [tx = 15 days after birth] when animals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively rapid transition to solid food reflects the altricial nature of the neonates and the need for accelerated growth in a seasonally productive environment. The 15-day weaning duration is consistent with values reported for other Sigmodon species and represents an intermediate pace among cricetid rodents. By the time of weaning, juveniles have more than doubled their birth mass and are capable of processing plant material, although maternal milk remains an important nutritional supplement during the final days of the nursing stage. The suckling juvenile period is characterized by rapid mass gain and the development of thermoregulatory capacity.

Sexual maturation in Sigmodon hirsutus occurs at approximately 40 days after birth [tp = approximately 40 days after birth] when individuals are housed at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This timing of puberty onset is based on extrapolations from the well-studied Sigmodon hispidus and reflects the relatively early sexual maturation typical of small-bodied rodents. At this age, females experience their first ovulation and males show testicular descent and active spermatogenesis. The attainment of reproductive maturity allows individuals born early in the breeding season to potentially contribute to reproduction within the same calendar year. This short generation time is an adaptation to environments where favorable conditions for reproduction are temporally constrained. The early onset of puberty contrasts with the ultimate body mass of 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams] reached later in life, indicating that reproductive capacity precedes full somatic growth.

Longevity in Sigmodon hirsutus is estimated at approximately 5.2 years [am = approximately 5.2 years] under controlled conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value inferred from the closely related Sigmodon hispidus. This lifespan is relatively long compared to many small-bodied cricetid rodents and suggests a life-history strategy characterized by sustained reproductive output over several seasons. The basal metabolic rate measured as maximal oxygen consumption reaches 184.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 184.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This elevated metabolic rate supports the high energetic demands of reproduction and thermoregulation in a species that inhabits both tropical and subtropical environments. The interplay between the estimated maximum lifespan, the 35-day gestation period (35 days) [tg = 35 days], and the single annual litter contributes to a relatively slow population turnover compared to smaller sympatric rodents, though the species remains capable of rapid population increases when conditions are favorable at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].
